# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Review: Varga & Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem"

Most of this comment is valuable. Sections 1–5 use the microdata to confirm, and put numbers on, the main weaknesses in the Halden pilot:

- **Attrition.** The withdrawal discrepancy is a serious finding. The working paper says organisations withdrew "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The exit forms show that seven of the nine withdrew after the schedule began, and six cited workload or output.
- **Manager rating.** Managers' indices exceeded the record-based figures in 19 of 23 organisations. A sign test on that split gives p ≈ 0.003, so the gap is systematic rather than noise.
- **Hours.** Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%. That is consistent with the 13% Varden found in its case-processing offices.
- **Revenue.** The revenue figure was nominal. Deflating it gives 1.014 / 1.041 ≈ 0.974, a real fall of about 2.6%.

Table 2's arithmetic checks: 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%, 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%.

The problems are in the abstract, sections 6–8, and the conclusion. The comment's evidence supports "the Halden gain is overstated by roughly half, and the remainder is uncertain". It concludes something much stronger.

## 1. The conclusion contradicts the best evidence the comment itself cites

The headline claim is that per-hour gains from reduced-hours schemes are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty". The comment calls the Varden trial the most reliable evidence available, but cites only its counter stratum.

Varden's case-processing stratum removes exactly the three problems the comment identifies:

- it was randomised, which addresses selection and attrition;
- it measured output from administrative records, which addresses manager rating;
- it used timesheet hours, which addresses the denominator.

It still found a gain of +12.5% per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4). Of the comment's four explanations, only novelty could apply to that result, and the comment offers no direct evidence of novelty (see §5 below). A reanalysis that calls one stratum of a trial the most reliable finding in the literature, and ignores the other stratum, which points the other way, is applying its standards selectively.

The calibration is also off in its own terms. The counter stratum has only 5 v 5 offices. Its confidence interval is wide, and conventional clustered standard errors are unreliable with that few clusters. It is good evidence, but "the most reliable finding in the literature to date" overstates it.

## 2. The abstract misdescribes the analysis

- **"Correcting the first three."** Table 2 corrects only two problems: the output measure and the hours denominator. Attrition is not corrected. All 17 organisations in the final row are survivors, and the comment never bounds the effect of the nine withdrawals.
- **"Four problems... account for most of the reported gain."** Revenue plays no part in the 23.4% calculation, so correcting it cannot account for any of the gain.
- **"Plausibly a novelty effect" becomes "entirely an artifact".** The abstract offers novelty as a plausible account of the residual. The conclusion then asserts that the gains are entirely artifact. Adding "in our assessment" doesn't make the stronger claim more supported.

## 3. Table 2 compares different subsets

The rows cover 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. The drop from 23.4% to 10.8% therefore mixes two things: the effect of the corrections, and differences in which organisations are included. Where the comparison can be done within a subset, the effect of the correction is clear. For the 23 organisations with records, the manager index of 98.9 implies +23.6% per scheduled hour, against +18.9% from records.

The key number is missing, though: the as-reported gain for the same 17 organisations in the last row. Without it, readers can't tell how much of the fall is due to correction and how much to subset composition. The Data note concedes this point, but the abstract and conclusion ignore it.

## 4. The hours decomposition doesn't add up

Section 3 reports baseline hours of 40.3 and pilot hours of 34.6. It attributes the gap between that and the scheduled 32 hours to two sources:

- longer remaining days, at +0.7 hours a day across four days, which is about 2.8 hours a week;
- work on the day off, at 1.6 hours a week.

Together those add about 4.4 hours to the 32 scheduled, which implies roughly 36.4 hours, not 34.6. On those figures, actual hours would have fallen by only about 9.5%. Either the per-day figure is wrong (about +0.25 a day would reconcile it) or the total is. This needs fixing, because the hours ratio drives the 10.8%.

## 5. The novelty argument is the weakest section, and it decides the conclusion

- **Arithmetic.** Energy fell from 0.61 SD at month three to 0.29 SD at month six, a decline of about 0.107 SD a month. Extrapolated linearly, it reaches zero at about month 8.7, not month 10. The bigger problem is that a linear extrapolation from two points is not a basis for prediction.
- **Energy is not output.** The argument assumes that falling self-reported energy means falling productivity. The microdata contains a *monthly* output index for every organisation. The authors could test directly whether output per hour declined over months three to six, and they don't report doing so.
- **Factual error.** The comment says staff "chose" the change. In the Halden pilot, participation was voluntary only at organisation level, and all staff in participating units moved to the new schedule.
- **Varden partly tests this.** Varden's control staff knew a trial was under way, and results held at nine months. That isn't conclusive, but it is evidence against a purely evaluation-driven effect, and the comment doesn't engage with it.
- **Burden of proof.** "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is a fair stance on durability. It supports "unproven", not "entirely an artifact".

## 6. The meetings section misdescribes the Varden trial and applies an uneven standard

- **Timing.** Varden collected the meeting data in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed. It was not "selected for analysis after the results were known".
- **Not a subgroup.** Case-processing was a stratum fixed before randomisation, not a post-hoc subgroup.
- **Not claimed as established.** Varden explicitly called the analysis unregistered, stressed that seven offices cannot establish a mechanism, said only that meetings "may account for part" of the gain, and registered a confirmatory test. The comment argues against a claim Varden did not make.
- **Uneven scepticism.** A correlation across seven offices (r = 0.71) is weak evidence; I said the same in my review of the trial. A linear extrapolation of a self-reported survey from two time points is weaker still. The comment rejects the first and builds its conclusion on the second.
- **The hypothesis cuts against the comment.** If cutting low-value meetings explains the gain, the gain is real. Removing unproductive hours is an improvement in per-hour productivity, not a measurement artifact.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Records as ground truth.** The comment treats record-based output as the true measure. But billable hours or tickets closed may miss outputs that a manager's index legitimately includes. "The manager index exceeds the records" is established; "overstates output" assumes the records are complete. Note too that organisations submitting records may differ from those that didn't.
- **Retail figure.** The −11.2% for retail and hospitality comes from three organisations. Lining it up with Varden's −11.4% is suggestive, but the two figures use different measures and draw on very small samples.
- **Uncertainty.** None of the corrected estimates has a confidence interval. With 17 organisations, the interval on 10.8% is likely wide.
- **Revenue.** The 4.1% CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue, and without a comparison group a fall in real revenue can't be attributed to the pilot either. The point that the 1.4% gave a misleading impression of growth still stands.
- **Scope.** The Data note says the estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole". The conclusion then generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" in general. The note is right and the conclusion contradicts it.

## What the comment supports

The comment's evidence supports these conclusions:

1. The Halden headline of +23.4% is substantially overstated. In the subsets where correction is possible, record-based output and actual hours imply roughly +11%, and attrition was not random and remains uncorrected.
2. The Halden paper's account of withdrawals is contradicted by its own microdata.
3. In coverage-bound work, reduced hours reduce output. Halden's corrected retail figures and Varden's counter stratum agree on this.
4. Whether any remaining per-hour gain lasts is unknown. The one randomised estimate free of measurement and selection problems (Varden's case-processing stratum) shows a gain at nine months, and its 24-month follow-up will be informative.

The recommendations in §8 are sound and match what Varden already did. The comment would be stronger if it:

- dropped "entirely";
- reported the within-subset comparisons and fixed the hours arithmetic;
- tested novelty using the monthly output data;
- either addressed Varden's case-processing result or explained why it doesn't apply.
